newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: FEATURE - Colombian agriculture sector in free fall.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Colombian agriculture sector in free fall.

text.p: Mounting violence in the countryside and a lowering of protectionist trade barriers are sounding the death knell for Colombia's once booming agricultural sector, experts say.

Agriculture Minister Alvaro Gomez has said a turnaround will be impossible without about $600 million in additional farm subsidies -- money the cash-strapped central government will be hard-pressed to deliver.
"The industry is in crisis," said Juan Manuel Ospina, who heads the Colombian Agricultural Society (SAC). "It is time that the nation faces up to reality."

Agricultural imports have skyrocketed by about 490 percent since the government began cutting tariffs and customs duties in 1990 as part of a move toward free-market policies known as "apertura." Cereal imports alone have soared 425 percent and livestock imports are up more than 1,000 percent.

The growing dependence on foreign foodstuffs is also due, at least in part, to the scant support local farmers receive from the government to compete with cheap imports. "The industry wasn't ready for openness," Adriano Quintana, head of the National Cereal Growers Federation, said.

As a result of rising costs and falling profits, Ospina said, Colombian growers have planted less land each year since 1990, culminating in a 2.7 percent drop in cultivation this year of two-season crops including wheat, potatoes and beans.
CULTIVATION CONTINUES TO DECLINE

Preliminary 1997 figures for some year-round products show the same trend. The value of sugar cane production fell 6.2 percent while palm oil production grew by a meagre 2.2 percent, about half the rate of the previous year.

Along with the lack of price supports and the flood of imports, agriculture experts say political violence has pushed a country that boasts some of the world's richest and most diverse farmland into growing dependence on foreign food.

"Violence is the greatest handicap to the industry," said Camilo Aldana, executive director of the Centre for Agricultural and Cattle Studies (CEGA) think-tank. "A complete recovery is not possible without peace," he added.

As recently as 1970, up to 80 percent of all Colombians lived in rural areas. Now roughly 80 percent live in cities, where people moved in droves to escape an increasingly brutal guerrilla war raging in the countryside.

Colombia's leftist rebel armies routinely kidnap and blackmail businessmen to fund Latin America's longest-running war. This violence and a backlash from right-wing paramilitary groups affects most of the agricultural sector, particularly cattle ranchers and sugarcane, palm and banana growers.
The National Cattlemen's Federation (FEDEGAN) said ranchers lost nearly $1 billion through rebel extortion and ransom payments and destroyed property last year alone.
"Some cattlemen can't even visit their ranches because of the danger," FEDEGAN president Jorge Visbal told a recent forum on rural violence.
HIGH PRICE OF NOT PAYING EXTORTION

Visbal said 60 percent of ranchers make rebel extortion payments, popularly known as "vaccines," which total more than $240,000 a year. The price for those who refuse to pay can be high -- rebels killed at least 47 cattle ranchers and kidnapped 511 last year.
Cattle production dropped 15 percent in the last 15 years, Visbal said, a fact that helps explain why imports of meat products have grown by about 200 percent since 1990.
Cheap imported goods have helped hold consumer food prices down but growers fear that dependence on imports will ultimately cost the country its entire agriculture industry.
"Do we want to be a country that can't provide its own food?" the cereal association's Qunitana asked.

Agricultural production fell by 3.5 percent in the first four months of 1997, preliminary figures from the government's National Statistics Department show. By some estimates, agriculture has lost more than 150,000 jobs since 1990.

There are no official figures on rural unemployment in Colombia but urban unemployment is at a nine-year high of 12.7 percent and analysts say many of the jobless are migrants from rural areas who live in the "rings of misery" that surround Colombia's cities.
